chapter: Left out of the jazz books; Tatum, Handy and family
title: Tatum's love of sports and memory for batting champions
summary: Collins describes track meets with Tatum and a Cleveland recording for a pilot's son while Tatum named a batting champion.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: Art Tatum: the legend, the piano and the man

blocks.x: We used to go -- we used to go to track meets, you know.
What did he get from a track meet? with (inaudible) 90 percent vision?

Well, hey, I would have to tell him what was happening, you know, but he would go to the track meet. He loved sports, you know, and he knew every record like baseball. He knew who the batting champ was in 1921, and we were in Cleveland playing a club there and he had a friend there who was a pilot, airline pilot, and he had known Art for quite a few years. And he invited us by his house this night, this afternoon before we went to -- we went over and had dinner, and he had a little boy, I guess around five or six, and he asked Art if he'd record something for his son. So Art said yes, so Art started playing and we -- in the meantime we had been discussing who's the batting champ, and

in some year, and he's telling me while he's playing, the batting champ, so and so and so and so. It was Joe Dimaggio. And he was right. And we played back this recording that he made and it was a masterpiece. It's just he had that kind of mind, you know.

So it was quite an experience being with him, and as I say I felt very closely -- I was very close to him, you know, and I was very, very, very fond of him. You know. So a lot of people -- I think of lot of musicians really knew him, though. Not too much has been written about him, but most of the musicians loved him and revered him, really. Because with all of that he was very earthy, you know. Like I wouldn't see him for a year, as soon as he got to town he would call me and it was just like I'd seen him yesterday. We'd take it from there, and we'd go.
